messages.subject: multiple parameterizations, Zero-inflated binomial and others
messages.subject_clean: multiple parameterizations, Zero-inflated binomial and others
messages.body_plain:
Apologize if this has been answered before but I did not find this issue specifically addressed in previous discussions.

INLA often offers multiple likelihood options for certain mixture distributions, like the zero-inflated families. For a given model and dataset, sometimes one of them will cause INLA to crash for me but one of the others often works just fine.  In this case, it is great to have multiple options, but just so I am clear: are these likelihoods generally expected to be equivalent in performance / accuracy?  Put another way, do these different likelihood specificiatons exist solely for reasons of convenience (i.e., just choose the one that works best for your problem) or is there some expectation that different parameterizations may in fact be more accurate for some problems,and thus good practice would be to always try each parameterization?

Many thanks,
Jonathan

On Sat, 2019-03-02 at 15:13 -0800, Jonathan Judge wrote:
> Apologize if this has been answered before but I did not find this
> issue specifically addressed in previous discussions.
>
> INLA often offers multiple likelihood options for certain mixture
> distributions, like the zero-inflated families. For a given model and
> dataset, sometimes one of them will cause INLA to crash for me but
> one of the others often works just fine.  In this case, it is great
> to have multiple options, but just so I am clear: are these
> likelihoods generally expected to be equivalent in performance /
> accuracy?  Put another way, do these different likelihood
> specificiatons exist solely for reasons of convenience (i.e., just
> choose the one that works best for your problem) or is there some
> expectation that different parameterizations may in fact be more
> accurate for some problems,and thus good practice would be to always
> try each parameterization?

Hi

I guess you're referring to type0/type1, where

	pI(y==0) + (1-p)*f(y)

or

	pI(y==0) + (1-p)*f(y|y>0)             (*)

They are ment to be for various situations depending on if the zero,
can come from the f() part or not. In the case where we have f(y|y>0),
then this is easier as it is well defined where a zero
comes from. In this case, we can also use a separate model for 'p', so
that p can depend on its own linear predictor, by fixing p in (*)
to (close to) zero, and represeting the right term in (*) with two
observations, first the binary with p(), then the response y from
f(y|y>0).

If one of them does not work in the sense of not converging, then using
a strong strong prior for p would really help, and then do a refit
starting from the fitted values,

r = inla(....with a strong prior, possible playing with the initial
value for p)

r = inla(..normal model goes here...,
         control.mode = list(result = r, restart = TRUE))

H

--
Håvard Rue

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to understand how the replicate effect works and my question is whether it is possible to have replicate'd effect of different lengths. For example, because they
are indexed over different sets. Is this possible?

I have just tried a model (modified from the FAQ) where I have three replicated effects, with the first one indexed from 1 to 50 and the other two from 1 to 100. It seems that I still get 100 points in the first random effect but it looks like as if the  the ones indexed from 51 to 100 are estimated assuming a missing response (which is what I would do if I had to keep all three replicated effects to have the same length).

I attach the code with my modified example.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] replicate effect
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] replicate effect
messages.body_plain:
Further to H:s response, the replicate feature is defined as a kronecker product, so yes, all replicates will have the same size, with “unused” components being predicted, as usual.

>From a theory perspective, allowing differently sized “replicates” should rather be thought of as “several independent models of the same general type, with different size but common hyperparameters”. For graph models, the size is an intrinsic part of the models itself; having differently sized “replicates” would involve a different graph for each “replicate”. Then the word “replicate” wouldn’t really be appropriate anymore.
So while the situation you describe commonly arises in e.g. time series modelling (with multiple time series realisations of different length from a common AR model), it’s not as easy to define in a generally applicable way through the general replicate feature.
For a specific model, defining an rgeneric model for the collection of “replicates” might be the easiest solution to reducing the memory requirements compared with the kronecker approach.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I’m working on a project trying to relate where fish live to features of the habitat. I have 12 different locations which are all roughly 10 x 20 m areas which are separated by between 250 m and 5 km. I’m trying to build a model using SPDE for this data and have a couple questions about how best to approach it. I’ve attached an R script to simulate something similar to my data and perform the analysis using the method of having a single mesh over the entire area with a finer scale within each site.

Thank you in advance for any advice you have for this!

Jason

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple iid spatial locations
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Multiple iid spatial locations
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

The case "relatively widely separate subregions where we care about
the within-subregion structure" you describe can be approached in
several ways,
but one way that is supported directly is to have a single mesh that
has disconnected components that cover each local region but allows
the same inla analysis code as if it was one connected component with
small triangles at the sites and large triangles connecting them. The
benefit of using disconnected components instead is that one can think
of it as having independent regions that just happen to be modelled
with the same spde parameters using different meshes, and need to
capture only the within-site structure. The between-site variability
can then be approached using other model components (that could be
spde models with only large triangles, or graph/network models, or iid
random effects, etc).

The "group" feature doesn't quite allow this, since it would require
the same mesh for each site; I couldn't work out what the _intent_ of
the code was; I'd need a more mathematical definition of the actual
model you want to implement; there's a lot of syntactically valid code
that implements _some_ model, but it's nicer to have it implement the
model we _want_. ;-)

Instead, to setup such a model you should only need to construct the
disconnected set of boundaries encircling each subregion, which the
inla.noncovex.hull() can do.
Provide points defining the subregions and a "convex" parameter that
gives appropriate domain extension (or if you have a multipolygon
defining the set of boundaries), and approach the mesh building as if
it was one connected domain, with extension of a suitable amount to
avoid boundary effects for each subdomain.

The main downside is that the semi-automated plotting features won't
easily show the local structure, as all subdomains will be plotted, so
you'll need to setup the plotting mapping coordinates more carefully.

It wasn't clear to me if you mentioned the "block" feature because you
think you need it or not? It can be used if your observations are
aggregated over the subregions (but to do that correctly for count
data isn't available yet; it's on our list to construct such
likelihoods in the inlabru package, as they turn into
not-quite-log-linear predictors). But if you're modelling the
structure within the subregions, as I assumed above, then you can
ignore that feature.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to get a deeper understanding on how the group options works. I have been able to find some great slides by Daniel Simpson and Andrea Riebler and, as far as I can understand, the group-ed latent effect would be defined as

f(idx, model = ...", ..., group = idx.group, control.group = list(model = "...", ...))

The resulting effect will be a GMRF with zero mean and precision

tau * Sigma_idx.group \otimes Sigma_idx

i.e., the Kronecker product between Sigma_idx.group  (the structure of the latent effect defined by the group index) and Sigma_idx (the structure of the latent effect define in the main f-function).

Also, matrices Sigma_idx.group and Sigma_idx will have any required parameter defined (e.g., an autocorrelation parameter in the ar1 models).

Is it necessary to include any other details in the definition of the group effects such as, for example, rank deficiency, sum-to-zero constraints, etc? I am just trying to think about what would happen when we have two intrinsic effects.

Many thanks.

Virgilio

messages.subject_clean: Discrepancy between random intercept precision and BLUP variance
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

The toy example below shows that lme4 and INLA yield comparable random intercept estimates. Yet the hyperparameter of the random intercept is very different. IMHO it doesn't match the estimates of the random intercept. Am I missing something?

Best regards,

Thierry

library(lme4)
library(INLA)
model_lme4 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1|Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(model_lme4) # random intercept variance = 1378, sigma = sqrt(var) = 37

model <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model = "iid"), data = sleepstudy)
to_sigma <- function(tau) {sqrt(1 / tau)}
inla.emarginal(to_sigma, model$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for Subject`) # sigma = 0.28
# naive sd on random intercepts sigma = 33.3
sd(model$summary.random$Subject[, 2])

plot(ranef(model_lme4)$Subject[, 1], model$summary.random$Subject[, 2])
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2)

messages.body_plain:
My focus is on the hyperparameter, not the sd of the individual estimates.

An iid random intercept follows x ~ N(0, \sigma_r). So I assume that sd(x) should be of the same magnitude as the hyperparameter \sigma_r.

In my toy example \sigma_r is calculated as inla.emarginal(function(tau) {sqrt(1 / tau)}, model$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for Subject`) and sd(x) as sd(model$summary.random$Subject[, "mean"]). sd(x) is about 100 times larger than \sigma_r, which seems strange to me.

I agree that the estimated \sigma_r depends on the prior. But regardless of the prior, I expect the magnitude of sd(x) to be similar of \sigma_r.

Best regards,

messages.body_plain:
The problem here is the default INLA prior.  When you use the so-called pc.prior, which usually produces much better estimates anyway in my experience, the results substantially match, with the INLA ones probably being more accurate since INLA is, in general, more accurate, all other things being equal. The pc.prior also has a much better marginal likelihood, confirming that it is probably more correct.

Code:

require(lme4)

require(INLA)

data("sleepstudy")

lme4.mod <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1|Subject), data=sleepstudy)

inla.1 <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model="iid"), data=sleepstudy)

summary(lme4.mod)

summary(inla.1) ### RE values quite different

bmod <- glm(Reaction ~ Days, data=sleepstudy)

sd_Base <- sd(residuals(bmod))

base.pc <- list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(3*sd_Base,0.01)))

inla.2 <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model="iid", hyper=base.pc), data=sleepstudy)

inla.2$summary.random

### compare random effect intercepts

cor(ranef(lme4.mod)[[1]][,1], inla.2$summary.random$Subject$mean) ## Rho of 1

##compare overall group effects

require(brinla)

VarCorr(lme4.mod)

bri.hyperpar.summary(inla.2) # very similar

H, what do you think about just making the pc.prior as specified above (which I think is what the original paper recommends) the default prior for “iid”?  It is easily automated to calculate through a function I think, and consistently produces better results in my experience, especially with smaller datasets.  It is the equivalent, apparently, of exponential(1), which others have contended is a best-practice default prior, something backed up by my experience. And getting results that are reasonably similar to what lme4 generates with its uniform priors seems important for accessibility to new users.

Jonathan

My focus is on the hyperparameter, not the sd of the individual estimates.

An iid random intercept follows x ~ N(0, \sigma_r). So I assume that sd(x) should be of the same magnitude as the hyperparameter \sigma_r.

In my toy example \sigma_r is calculated as inla.emarginal(function(tau) {sqrt(1 / tau)}, model$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for Subject`) and sd(x) as sd(model$summary.random$Subject[, "mean"]). sd(x) is about 100 times larger than \sigma_r, which seems strange to me.

I agree that the estimated \sigma_r depends on the prior. But regardless of the prior, I expect the magnitude of sd(x) to be similar of \sigma_r.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Your last sentence unfortunately isn’t correct; conditionally on the variance parameters, the posterior mean of the latent Gaussian variables tend to depend only on the ratio between the latent effect variance and the observation noise variance; the absolute variance is only seen in the posterior variances for the x:s. In spatial models, this can be seen by noting that the kriging estimate is invariant to the variance, as long as the ratio between the variances is kept constant.
This means that strong priors can in principle give the effect you describe.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am struggling to understand the meaning of the credible intervals from a binomial (bernoulli) bayesian regression model. I think that secchi.std, Phos.std, and Nit.std are not important because their intervals include 0.

The rest of the variables appear important because their intervals do not include 0. salinity.std has a negative effect on the response variable, as does distance.between.beds.std.

neighbors.std, total.area.std, and distance.to.edge.std have positive effects on the response.

Is that correct, or am I mixed up?

Also, is there a way to figure out the threshold value of each important covariate above/below which the response is a 1 (success)?

If I standardized my covariates before running the model, do I need to transform these credible intervals in any way?

Thanks!

-Carrie

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] interpreting credible intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carrie,

Your question is quite complex, because "it depends". And to be helpful, I would have to describe in detail how it depends on each thing, and what the interpretation is. At which point I would have written an introductory book to Bayesian inference.

I hope you are not too offended if I say that you cannot expect a detailed response on this topic in this email list. If you have a question about what a number mean, you can expect us to tell you, e.g that it is the quantiles of the credible interval. But if you want to know what a credible interval is, there are other resources you should use.

Asking for recommended literature is natural in this email list. If this is what you want, I recommend the books under
http://www.r-inla.org/books
and the other applied statistical introductions by Zuur. But I have not read them in detail, so I cannot provide a more precise recommendation.

Kind regards,
Haakon

Hi Rujia,

I have been working on this topic extensively!

This will take significantly more time to compute than using the mesh you have attached. The mesh you have attached would be considered too coarse also in the stationary case.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] link=1 in control.predictor
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] link=1 in control.predictor
messages.body_plain:
For multi-likelihood models, you need to set the link parameter to a vector, where each value indicates which of the link functions to use, for each data/prediction point.
E.g. if your response matrix has 3 rows for likelihood 1 and 5 rows for likelihood 2, followed by 4 rows of NA for predicting two points on the linked scale for each likelihood, link should be set to
c(1,1,1,2,2,2,2,2,1,1,2,2)

link=1 is just shorthand for “apply the first link function to everything”.

Finn

On Monday, January 7, 2019 at 8:12:17 PM UTC+8, Joaquin Cavieres wrote:
> Hi everyone
>
> I think that the next link can be of help
>
> https://spark.rstudio.com/guides/distributed-r/
>
> Regards!
>
> El lunes, 7 de enero de 2019, 7:36:34 (UTC-3), Virgilio Gómez-Rubio escribió:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I am very interested on this. I am not an expert on Spark but I can help by providing examples and testing them on spark.
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Virgilio
> >
> > El jue., 3 ene. 2019 a las 9:50, <harr...@mobike.com> escribió:
> > > `sparklyr::spark_apply` function seems can replace `mcapply` function to parallel INLA program, I am new bees for INLA, but mastering more about sparklyr. Does anyone be interesting in this?
> > >
> > > On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 7:20:36 PM UTC+8, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > I know that this is a "cold" thread but I would like to share some thoughts on this. We have done some work to fit unimplemented models in R-INLA by fitting several models with R-INLA where some parameters had been fixed (so that the model could be fitted with R-INLA) and then combining all the resulting models using Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA).
> > > >
> > > > The idea is that if we have a model that is not implemented in R-INLA but that could be fitted by fixing one or a few parameters, then we could take different values of this ensemble of parameters over a grid, fit the conditional models (on the values of these parameters) and then combine them together using BMA. If the model is already available in R-INLA it may be faster to run simpler models and then combine them, depending on the amount of data we have.
> > > >
> > > > I am not sure if this would qualify as a Map-Reduce algorithm. The Map part would be splitting the whole model into (simpler) conditional models and the Reduce step would be to put all the model outputs together to get the desired (and more complex) model.
> > > >
> > > > We have some code in the INLABMA that could me summarised as:
> > > >
> > > > #Define grid on nuisance parameter rho
> > > > rrho<-seq(0, .95, length.out=40)
> > > >
> > > > #Fit condintioned models by fixing the value of rho
> > > > #sem.inla() uses RINLA to fit a model given the value of rho
> > > > #MAP step (?)
> > > >
> > > >  seminla<-mclapply(rrho, function(rho){
> > > >                           sem.inla(form, d=columbus, W=W, rho=rho, ...)
> > > >      })
> > > >
> > > > #Put all the models together to get our original model
> > > > #REDUCE step (?)
> > > > sembma<-INLABMA(seminla, rrho, 0)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Conditional models are fitted in parallel using mclapply(). If data are distributed over different nodes, I do not think this approach could handle it, but it could deal with large datasets in one node because we are fitting simpler models. Combining the models only involves computing a weighted sum of matrices (e.g., the matrices representing the posterior marginals) and it can also be done very fast and in parallel.
> > > >
> > > > Not sure if this makes sense, but any comments on this are welcome.
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > >
> > > > Virgilio
> > > >
> > > > P.S: This approach is detailed in Bivand et al. (2014), Spatial Statistics journal. You can also check the INLABMA package to get the full example that I have mentioned.
> > > >
> > > > 2015-07-19 21:32 GMT+02:00 Håvard Rue <hr...@math.ntnu.no>:
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm happy to discuss this, maybe best outside this list.
> > > > >
> > > > > Håvard
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Fri, 2015-07-17 at 21:14 -0700, David Boney wrote:
> > > > > > Has anyone written an algorithms or architecture paper on R-INLA?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am new to R-INLA. I have read the paper by Rue, Martino, and Chopin
> > > > > > (2009) and the paper by Martins, Simpson, Lindgren, and Rue (2013). I
> > > > > > am wanting to learn the software architecture and what algorithms are
> > > > > > used in both R-INLA and the underlying GMRFlib. I get the gist of the
> > > > > > method from the papers but I am at a disadvantage, being a computer
> > > > > > scientist, in understanding the details of the algorithms and their
> > > > > > implementation. I suspect I will have to read the source code and
> > > > > > reverse engineer the architecture.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am interested in building a Bayesian model solver for big data
> > > > > > sets. To make this concrete, let's start simple with Bayesian linear
> > > > > > regression with a data set that has ten billion rows and a hundred
> > > > > > real valuated covariates and ten thousand sparse indicator
> > > > > > covariates. I just made up this example to given an example that will
> > > > > > never fit in R. I am interested in studying INLA to see if it can be
> > > > > > solved with the Map-Reduce paradigm use in Spark, an open source
> > > > > > distributed computing system. Two areas where there are known
> > > > > > parallel methods with Map-Reduce algorithms for big data sets are
> > > > > > numerical linear algebra and convex optimization. I am interested in
> > > > > > learning how INLA uses linear algebra and if the various optimization
> > > > > > steps are convex optimization problems. One area that has been very
> > > > > > useful for big data are randomized numerical linear algebra
> > > > > > algorithms. These algorithms can invert a nxm matrix in O(n x m x
> > > > > > log(m)). Being yet another approximation in the algorithms, it is
> > > > > > unknown how the approximation error would propagate through the
> > > > > > algorithms.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > What I would like to build is an open source Bayesian solver to
> > > > > > contribute to the MLIB package in the Spark distribution. I am happy
> > > > > > to correspond with anyone who is interested.
> > > > > >

leave-out-one-at-the-time is there already. If you want to leave out
more, you can do that in the loop, and set a selection of theresponse
to NA. recall to set them back afterwards. this will create predictions
for the ones you leave out.

if you look at the code for

	inla.cpo

you can use the control.mode=list(result=r, restart=T)

trick to make it run a bit faster, and also you can turn off to compute
those marginals you will not need.

I am fitting a spatial BYM model to small areal unit data, using:

formula <- Y ~ 1 + f(id,model = "bym",graph = g)
mod <- inla(formula,family = "nbinomial",data = dat,E = E)

Can INLA utilise a non-symmetric adjacency matrix? This models fits in 2 minutes when g is symmetric, but endlessly reports "Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it..." if g is not symmetric.

An example of where one may wish to utilise a non-symmetric adjacency is when the neighbourhood of each polygon comprises nearby polygons up to a target (minimum) population size. In this scenario it may arise that polygon i is a neighbour of j, but not vice versa.

>From my reading the FAQ "Some of the models needs a graph, how do I specify it?" suggests that it is required that the adjacency matrix is symmetric. Can anyone confirm this?

Thanks,
Matt

unscaled version of the bym is not generally 'good', and you should use
model="bym2" instead, or at least add argument scale.model=TRUE for the
bym. (this is required for bym2)

  year =         2018,
  keywords =     {year2018,my.own,my.cv <http://my.cv>},

in any case it will end up with a symmetric precision (covariance)
matrix, so if you want to use a non-symmetric one, there is also a
symmetric choice that give the same result...  so I don't what you will
gain really.

At each point on a reef within a site I have the number of a species of fish and a handful of covariates relating to the reef structure. Most often there are no fish present, so I want to model the size and presence of the schools of fish using a hurdle model (for the sake of this example I’m using a fixed zero inflation factor but in the final model I’ll model both the presence/absence and the count when present). This model will be based on the measured covariates of the reef along with a random effect of site and a term for the spatial structure which is allowed to vary among sites.

I believe this describes the model I’m trying to fit but I’m definitely still learning how to do all this so please forgive any glaring mistakes!

i = individual data points (1, 2, ..., 2500)

k = sites (1, 2, 3, 4)

j = covariates (0, 1, 2)

y_ik ~ ZIP (lambda_i, pi)

eta_i ~ beta_0 + beta_1 * X_1i + beta_2 * X_2i + mu_ik + gamma_ik

beta_j ~ N(0, 0.001 ^ -1)

gamma_ik ~ GF (0, sigma_k)

sigma_k = Matern covariance

mu_ik ~ N(0, 0.001 ^ -1)

pi ~ U(0, 1)

Jason

> Hi!

> The case "relatively widely separate subregions where we care about
> the within-subregion structure" you describe can be approached in
> several ways,
> but one way that is supported directly is to have a single mesh that
> has disconnected components that cover each local region but allows
> the same inla analysis code as if it was one connected component with
> small triangles at the sites and large triangles connecting them. The
> benefit of using disconnected components instead is that one can think
> of it as having independent regions that just happen to be modelled
> with the same spde parameters using different meshes, and need to
> capture only the within-site structure. The between-site variability
> can then be approached using other model components (that could be
> spde models with only large triangles, or graph/network models, or iid
> random effects, etc).
>
> The "group" feature doesn't quite allow this, since it would require
> the same mesh for each site; I couldn't work out what the _intent_ of
> the code was; I'd need a more mathematical definition of the actual
> model you want to implement; there's a lot of syntactically valid code
> that implements _some_ model, but it's nicer to have it implement the
> model we _want_. ;-)
>
> Instead, to setup such a model you should only need to construct the
> disconnected set of boundaries encircling each subregion, which the
> inla.noncovex.hull() can do.
> Provide points defining the subregions and a "convex" parameter that
> gives appropriate domain extension (or if you have a multipolygon
> defining the set of boundaries), and approach the mesh building as if
> it was one connected domain, with extension of a suitable amount to
> avoid boundary effects for each subdomain.
>
> The main downside is that the semi-automated plotting features won't
> easily show the local structure, as all subdomains will be plotted, so
> you'll need to setup the plotting mapping coordinates more carefully.
>
> It wasn't clear to me if you mentioned the "block" feature because you
> think you need it or not? It can be used if your observations are
> aggregated over the subregions (but to do that correctly for count
> data isn't available yet; it's on our list to construct such
> likelihoods in the inlabru package, as they turn into
> not-quite-log-linear predictors). But if you're modelling the
> structure within the subregions, as I assumed above, then you can
> ignore that feature.

messages.subject: How exactly to hyperpriors on "group=" interaction work?
messages.subject_clean: How exactly to hyperpriors on "group=" interaction work?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have questions about the meaning of precision hyperpriors in "group=" interaction models that I couldn't find answers to.

Say I have a space-time interaction term where I specify a PC prior for both the space and time parts independently, such as

f(space, model='besag', graph=neighborGraph, hyper=list(prec = list( prior = "pc.prec", param = 0.2, alpha = 0.01)),
       group = time, control.group=list(model="rw2", hyper =list(prec = list( prior = "pc.prec", param = 0.2, alpha = 0.01)) ))).

When I fit the model, everything runs fine and gives reasonable answers, but in the hyperparameters summary, inla.fit$summary.hyper, I only see a summary stats for the posterior precision of the "space" effect but not "time."  It would make sense to me that INLA only fits one precision parameter for the kronecker product of space+time, but the ability to specify priors separately makes me wonder if instead I'm just missing a control.group option (or control.?) to output the time precision posterior.

Questions:
Does INLA just estimate one precision parameter to scale the kronecker-producted interaction?
If yes, then how are the two partial priors combined?
If no, then where can I find the posterior for the group model precision?
Thanks!

--Mike

The bym models are defined for undirected graphs, not just in the software, but in general theory. It sounds like you want some kind of semi-directed graph model, as that’s what an asymmetric adjacency matrix would imply? Just taking the conditional distributions from the bym definition and applying them to a directed graph doesn’t necessarily give a valid model.

I’m don’t have the documentation in front of me, but I think the “symmetric” option simply uses both upper and lower parts of the adjacency to define the graph, ie symmetrise it, and otherwise just uses either the upper or lower triangle, which may give a different undirected graph?

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA utilise a non-symmetric adjacency matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, it’s a long known issue. With a DAG everything is fine but as soon as the directed graph has cycles you have to be careful to ensure a valid model. The basic CAR model can be defined via pairwise potentials on undirected graphs. I suspect other models on partially directed graphs (I.e. with asymmetric adjacency I some sense) with cycles can be built by looking at clique potentials of the undirected “moralized” graph, but haven’t given that any real thought; in any event you should simply end up with slightly different coefficients, but still a CAR model (since _all_ linear Gaussian models are (nonstationary) CAR models on some graph...)

Finn

Thank you all for your replies.

I think I understand now that the CAR specification in the BYM requires an undirected graph (corresponding to a symmetric neighbour matrix) by construction. Thus the errors I see are not due to a failure of the algorithms within inla(). I'm not sure which 'symmetric' option you are referring to - is this somewhere in inla()?

My background is applied so the theory being discussed is getting hard to follow. However my questoin is now: does INLA provide for a similar model specification to the BYM, but which allows for such a semi-directed graph specification of neighbours? A common example might be where neighbours for each polygon are defined by k-nearest neighbours (knn). A knn specification of neighbours also gives a non-symmetric neighbour matrix. To fit this I would try the below code, which I have confirmed gives similar errors to those I first described. However, papers such as Morrison et al. (2011) (cited below) suggest that such a model is possible. They conducted a sensitivity analysis comparing "first-order contiguity, second-order contiguity, four nearest neighbors, and eight nearest neighbors", using a CAR specification.

Apologies if these questions have already been answered in this thread.

Thank you,
Matt

mod_bym <- inla(f_bym,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,verbose = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
there is an issue here with adjacency matrix A, and the precision
matrix Q. as Q = AA' (plus some other terms), then Q is symmetric, and
if A is non-symmetric there exists a symmetric B, so that BB' = AA'

so if your input require a non-symmetric A, then we have to make sure
that the non-symmetry gets preserved through the code. the easiest
then, is the write this a rgeneric function, see inla.doc("rgeneric")
where you control every detail yourself.

H

messages.body_plain:
To clarify what's going on here a bit further, what Haavard just
described is a SAR model (simultaneous autoregression) on the original
graph.

Proper CAR models are defined through first and second order clique
potentials on undirected graphs, i.e.
  -2 \log p(x) = const + \sum_i a_i x_i^2 + \sum_{(i,j); j~i} b_{ij}
(x_i - x_j)^2
       = const + \sum_ij x_i Q_ij x_j
in terms relating to the Hammersley-Clifford theorem (disclaimer for
possible pair-miscounting etc),
for some Q_{ij}, that are defined by the a_i and b_ij values, and Q_ij
= 0 unless i~j or i=j.
Intrinsic CAR models have a_i = 0 for all i but otherwise work the same.
The most common CAR models have b_ij = \tau = const for all pairs i~j.

This has the consequence that the full conditional distributions are
  (x_i | x_j, j \neq i) ~ N( \sum_j c_ij x_j, Q_ii^{-1} ),
where c_ij = -Q_ij / Q_ii .
What we can _not_ do is to mandate c_ij = -Q_ij/Q_ii values
arbitrarily, since that would not
necessarily define a symmetric positive definite precision matrix Q.

Now, let be an asymmetric adjacency matrix A and we want the
interpretation to be
that node i "collects" information from its directed neighbours
specified in row i.
(take A' if the interpretation of the arrows is the opposite)
Let B be the rowwise normalised version such that the rowsums are equal to 1
(I assume all nodes have at least one neighbour).

Then we can write a model on matrix form with x as the vector of
variables, and e independent N(0,1) noise:
  x = rho Bx + e
where -1 < rho < 1. (rho = 1 would give an intrinsic model)
The interpretation is that the value at a node is a scaled average of
it's directed neighbours, plus noise.

Rearrange terms to
  (I - rho B) x = e

This is a simultaneous autoregression model of order 1 on the
undirected version of the graph, SAR(1).
The covariances of the left and right hand sides must match:
  (I - rho B) Sigma (I - rho B)' = I, where Sigma is the covariance for x.
Inverting and rearranging factors gives the precision for x,
  Q = (I - rho B)' (I - rho B)

The resulting SAR model is a CAR(2) model on the undirected version of
the original graph,
but has a clear motivation in terms of the asymmetric directed graph.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Sorry, some corrections to my own post:

The last comment about the result being a CAR(2) model only refers to
the case where the directed model is symmetric. When it's asymmetric,
it depends on the actual graph structure what kind of CAR model it is
(and on what undirected graph).

For example, if the directed graph describes a time chain, the SAR
model will define an ordinary temporal AR(1) model, which can also be
seen as a CAR(1) model on the undirected version of the graph.

For general asymmetric graphs, the model will be somewhere inbetween
CAR(1) and CAR(2), depending on the details of the local graph
structure.

Finn

On Thursday, March 14, 2019 at 7:21:35 PM UTC+8, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Sorry, some corrections to my own post:
>
> The last comment about the result being a CAR(2) model only refers to
> the case where the directed model is symmetric. When it's asymmetric,
> it depends on the actual graph structure what kind of CAR model it is
> (and on what undirected graph).
>
> For example, if the directed graph describes a time chain, the SAR
> model will define an ordinary temporal AR(1) model, which can also be
> seen as a CAR(1) model on the undirected version of the graph.
>
> For general asymmetric graphs, the model will be somewhere inbetween
> CAR(1) and CAR(2), depending on the details of the local graph
> structure.
>
> Finn
>
> On Thu, 14 Mar 2019 at 11:01, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > To clarify what's going on here a bit further, what Haavard just
> > described is a SAR model (simultaneous autoregression) on the original
> > graph.
> >
> > Proper CAR models are defined through first and second order clique
> > potentials on undirected graphs, i.e.
> >   -2 \log p(x) = const + \sum_i a_i x_i^2 + \sum_{(i,j); j~i} b_{ij}
> > (x_i - x_j)^2
> >        = const + \sum_ij x_i Q_ij x_j
> > in terms relating to the Hammersley-Clifford theorem (disclaimer for
> > possible pair-miscounting etc),
> > for some Q_{ij}, that are defined by the a_i and b_ij values, and Q_ij
> > = 0 unless i~j or i=j.
> > Intrinsic CAR models have a_i = 0 for all i but otherwise work the same.
> > The most common CAR models have b_ij = \tau = const for all pairs i~j.
> >
> > This has the consequence that the full conditional distributions are
> >   (x_i | x_j, j \neq i) ~ N( \sum_j c_ij x_j, Q_ii^{-1} ),
> > where c_ij = -Q_ij / Q_ii .
> > What we can _not_ do is to mandate c_ij = -Q_ij/Q_ii values
> > arbitrarily, since that would not
> > necessarily define a symmetric positive definite precision matrix Q.
> >
> > Now, let be an asymmetric adjacency matrix A and we want the
> > interpretation to be
> > that node i "collects" information from its directed neighbours
> > specified in row i.
> > (take A' if the interpretation of the arrows is the opposite)
> > Let B be the rowwise normalised version such that the rowsums are equal to 1
> > (I assume all nodes have at least one neighbour).
> >
> > Then we can write a model on matrix form with x as the vector of
> > variables, and e independent N(0,1) noise:
> >   x = rho Bx + e
> > where -1 < rho < 1. (rho = 1 would give an intrinsic model)
> > The interpretation is that the value at a node is a scaled average of
> > it's directed neighbours, plus noise.
> >
> > Rearrange terms to
> >   (I - rho B) x = e
> >
> > This is a simultaneous autoregression model of order 1 on the
> > undirected version of the graph, SAR(1).
> > The covariances of the left and right hand sides must match:
> >   (I - rho B) Sigma (I - rho B)' = I, where Sigma is the covariance for x.
> > Inverting and rearranging factors gives the precision for x,
> >   Q = (I - rho B)' (I - rho B)
> >
> > The resulting SAR model is a CAR(2) model on the undirected version of
> > the original graph,
> > but has a clear motivation in terms of the asymmetric directed graph.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> >
> > On Thu, 14 Mar 2019 at 05:26, Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > >
> > > there is an issue here with adjacency matrix A, and the precision
> > > matrix Q. as Q = AA' (plus some other terms), then Q is symmetric, and
> > > if A is non-symmetric there exists a symmetric B, so that BB' = AA'
> > >
> > > so if your input require a non-symmetric A, then we have to make sure
> > > that the non-symmetry gets preserved through the code. the easiest
> > > then, is the write this a rgeneric function, see inla.doc("rgeneric")
> > > where you control every detail yourself.
> > >
> > > H
> > >
> > > On Wed, 2019-03-13 at 19:44 +0000, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > > Yes, it’s a long known issue. With a DAG everything is fine but as
> > > > soon as the directed graph has cycles you have to be careful to
> > > > ensure a valid model. The basic CAR model can be defined via pairwise
> > > > potentials on undirected graphs. I suspect other models on partially
> > > > directed graphs (I.e. with asymmetric adjacency I some sense) with
> > > > cycles can be built by looking at clique potentials of the undirected
> > > > “moralized” graph, but haven’t given that any real thought; in any
> > > > event you should simply end up with slightly different coefficients,
> > > > but still a CAR model (since _all_ linear Gaussian models are
> > > > (nonstationary) CAR models on some graph...)
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > > On 13 Mar 2019, at 19:34, Aniruddha Banerjee <
> > > > aniruddha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > This is a very interesting topic and maybe the Hammersley Clifford
> > > > > Theorem might help ... (
> > > > > https://repository.upenn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1162&context=cis_papers
> > > > > ) -Rudy
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Mar 13, 2019 at 12:40 AM Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > > > > > On Tue, 2019-03-12 at 20:16 -0700, Matt Tuson wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Havard,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I'm not sure if I am encountering a 'non pos def matrix' error.
> > > > > > Is
> > > > > > > this what the Fail to factorize Q message is implying?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > this is exactly this.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > if you input a non-symmetric graph/matrix, I am not sure what
> > > > > > will
> > > > > > happen, as the assumption is that its symmetric, so it depends on
> > > > > > how
> > > > > > the code is written how this non-symmetric input is interpreted.
> > > > > >

messages.subject: How to specify nested random effects?
messages.subject_clean: How to specify nested random effects?
messages.body_plain:
I have count data from multiple sites (e.g. S1, S2, S3, S4) which are located in two areas ("north", "south"), with a pile of continuous covariates, and multiple years (modelled with "rw2").

How would I specify the model to indicate that sites 1 & 2 are always in "north" area and sites 3 & 4 are always in "south" area ?

I've tried the following specifications (leaving out model = "iid" from each term for clarity):

f1 = count ~ f(area) + f(site) + cov
f2 = count ~ f(area, site) + cov
f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(area2, site) + cov  # area2 being a duplicate of area
f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(site, area2) + cov

In lme4 I'd specify: count ~ cov + (1 | area / site)

Which, if any, is the correct INLA specification?

(Please excuse the basic question--I'm brand new to R-INLA, but enjoying it so far!)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it depends on what precisely the "nested" aspect should mean; someone
with familiarity of lme4 might have a clearer answer to this,
but my understanding is that "(1 | area / site)" is equivalent to "(1
| area) + (1 | area:site)". However, the interaction term "area:site"
seems to me to be equivalent to just "site", since each site can only
be located within one of your two areas. That would indicate that
f(area) + f(site) is what you need.

An exception to that would be if the lme4 "(1 | area:site)" implies
that each area should have its own variance parameter for the
area:site effect. If that's the case, I believe you would need
to split the site index vector into site1 and site2; if
  area = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2)
and
 site <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
let
 site1 <- site2 <- site
 site1[area != 1] <- NA # site1: c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, NA, NA)
 site2[area != 2] <- NA # site1: c(NA, NA, 3, NA, 5, 6, 7)
and use
 f(area) + f(site1, n = 7) + f(site2, n = 7)
in the formula, so that each area gets it's own iid-precision
parameter for the site effects.

For a smaller computational model the site indices within site1 and
site2 should be compressed into
 site1: c(1, 2, NA, 3, NA, NA, NA)
 site2: c(NA, NA, 1, NA, 2, 3, 4)
and the "n" parameters to f can be removed.

If there are no repeated measurements, this is easily done:
 site1 <- site2 <- site
 site1[area != 1] <- NA
 site2[area != 2] <- NA
 site1[area == 1] <- seq_len(sum(area == 1))
 site2[area == 2] <- seq_len(sum(area == 2))

If there _are_ repeated measurements, more care needs to be taken when
renumbering the sites, so that all observations for a site is mapped
to the same new index.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Error message clarification
messages.body_plain:
Just to post on quick update on this.

It turns out that the model needed to be specified using Ntrials in the call to INLA to speed up the calculation. The high number of non-unique cases in the relatively large dataset was making the computation difficult, ultimately resulting in the error above.

Reformatting the dataset to only include unique rows and a column containing the number of repeats for each works perfectly.

When specifying Y for this model, note that it needs to be the sum of the original Ys. For example, in the case of a binomial model, that means that it is either 0, or Ntrials (1 * number of cases).

Thanks again for all the help!

messages.body_plain:
I am considering a LGCP with intensity surface given by

log( lamda(s) ) = beta_0 + x(s)beta _1+ eta(s)

where, eta(s) is a Gaussian random field and x(s) is the Euclidean distance to fixed location on the map. When fitting this model via MCMC, following the SPDE approach for the random effect, it is clear that the fixed effects and random effect are confounded.

How is INLA handling spatial confounding for LGCP fits with spatially continuous covariates?

Best,
Adam

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Confounding in LGCP
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial Confounding in LGCP
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Short answer: it doesn’t do anything.
It’s up to the user to define a model that has the kind of interpretability properties that are desired. Unfortunately, it’s an open question whether that’s always possible.

One approach is to impose an orthogonality constraint between the covariate(s) and the random field component on the domain the lgcp is defined on. This can be done via the linear integral constraint options in inla.spde2.matern.

Another option is to do a post processing constraint where the covariate-like aspects of the spde are subtracted and moved into the covariate effect.

A third option is to specify covariance parameters for the spde that encourages it to avoid spatial structure of the size present in the covariate.

A fourth option is to accept the harsh truth that only the combined effect of the covariate and field are identifiable. (This is an important option!)

Which of these, or other, options to use depend on the precise problem and scientific questions that are of interest.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: INLA model evaluation
messages.subject_clean: INLA model evaluation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephen,

There are lots of ways to judge fit and compare models using R-INLA. The options depend on a lot of factors, including the type of model. For the sake of discussion, consider a Poisson regression model.

Here is some R code to play with. It makes some data, defines some models, fits the models, evaluates model fit by extracting fitted values and PIT values, and compares the predictive performance of models with WAIC and logarithmic scores from CPO values. Hope that helps. A link to further reading is at the bottom.

# load libraries
library(INLA)
library(brinla)
library(ggplot2)

# make Poisson regression data (code from Marc Kery)
# represents bird counts over many years at several sites
n.groups <- 16
n.years <- 30
n <- n.groups * n.years
pop <- gl(n = n.groups, k = n.years)
original.year <- rep(1:n.years, n.groups)
year <- (original.year-1)/29
Xmat <- model.matrix(~pop*year-1-year)
intercept.mean <- 3
intercept.sd <http://intercept.sd> <- 1
slope.mean <- -2
slope.sd <http://slope.sd> <- 0.6
intercept.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=intercept.mean, sd=intercept.sd <http://intercept.sd>)
slope.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=slope.mean, sd=slope.sd <http://slope.sd>)
all.effects <- c(intercept.effects, slope.effects)
lin.pred <- Xmat[,] %*% all.effects
C <- rpois(n=n, lambda=exp(lin.pred))
dat1 <- data.frame(count=C, year=original.year, population=pop, rand_int=pop,
                   rand_slope=pop)
ggplot(dat1, (aes(x=year, y=count))) + geom_point () +
  facet_wrap(~population, scales="free") + geom_smooth()

# write models
form1 <- count ~ year
form2 <- count ~ year +
  f(rand_int, model="iid",
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))))
form3 <- count ~ year +
  f(rand_int, model="iid",
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
  f(rand_slope, year, model="iid",
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))))

# fit models
fix_only_pois <- inla(form1, data=dat1, family="poisson",
             control.compute=list(waic=T, cpo=T))
fix_only_nb <- inla(form1, data=dat1, family="nbinomial",
             control.compute=list(waic=T, cpo=T))
rand_int_pois <- inla(form2, data=dat1, family="poisson",
             control.compute=list(waic=T, cpo=T))
rand_int_slope_pois <- inla(form3, data=dat1, family="poisson",
             control.compute=list(waic=T, cpo=T))

# look at model summaries
summary(fix_only_pois)
summary(fix_only_nb)
summary(rand_int_pois); bri.hyperpar.summary(rand_int_pois)
summary(rand_int_slope_pois); bri.hyperpar.summary(rand_int_slope_pois)

# look at observed versus fitted for model fit
qplot(fix_only_pois$summary.fitted.values$mean, dat1$count) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0)
qplot(fix_only_nb$summary.fitted.values$mean, dat1$count) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0)
qplot(rand_int_pois$summary.fitted.values$mean, dat1$count) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0)
qplot(rand_int_slope_pois$summary.fitted.values$mean, dat1$count) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0)

# look at PIT histograms for uniformity for model fit
qplot(fix_only_pois$cpo$pit, geom="histogram")
qplot(fix_only_nb$cpo$pit, geom="histogram")
qplot(rand_int_pois$cpo$pit, geom="histogram")
qplot(rand_int_slope_pois$cpo$pit, geom="histogram")

# compare models with waic
fix_only_pois$waic$waic
fix_only_nb$waic$waic
rand_int_pois$waic$waic
rand_int_slope_pois$waic$waic

# compare models with the logarithmic score
-mean(log(fix_only_pois$cpo$cpo))
-mean(log(fix_only_nb$cpo$cpo))
-mean(log(rand_int_pois$cpo$cpo))
-mean(log(rand_int_slope_pois$cpo$cpo))

# see more here on model criticism and selection:
# http://doc.rero.ch/record/313537/files/180_2010_Article_208.pdf

messages.subject: Optimizing runs using GPU or CPUs / Hitting limits with OpenMP multithreading
messages.subject_clean: Optimizing runs using GPU or CPUs / Hitting limits with OpenMP multithreading
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA users and developers!

I have been recently experimenting with seeing how much I can push INLA to do faster computation and I have a bunch of questions that spawned up. For background I compile INLA from source in Linux machines.

It's been a super interesting rabbit hole that I went down on, so thank you so much if you could happen to help me out with my questions below!!

1) BLAS/LAPACK linking: When INLA is running, does it only rely on the BLAS/LAPACK library that is provided at build-time? I compiled R against the Intel MKL BLAS/LAPACK libraries, and so, I'm wondering if I need to explicitly have anything in the INLA Makefile, except for `-L` library flags pointing to where the MKL shared objects are.

2) blas.num.threads: Suppose that I built INLA by successfully linking against the MKL libraries, and R is also loaded up with the proper Intel MKL BLAS/LAPACK (which I can confirm from sessionInfo()). Would having the `blas.num.threads` option set to something more than 1 get INLA to use MKL threading?

3) On the topic of parallelization: I have seen in simple examples that if I set `num.threads` to more than 1, then INLA will use OpenMP threading to fit a model, and that can be faster. However, it looks like when I have a model with a large spatial region and therefore a large number of random effects, INLA will segfault if I set OpenMP to more than 1. I have tried this on a machine with 1TB of memory.

My assumption here is that: as we set higher number of `num.threads` to, let's say, 4, INLA will try to estimate 4 times the number of parameters and therefore, there might be some internal limits to the number of parameters that is being hit, even though the memory limit is not being reached at all. Is that a correct assumption? And if so, do you have any other suggestions of speeding up the computation beyond just jacking up OpenMP threading?

4) Finally, GPUs! : Ultimately, the end goal of this research for me is to see how much I can speed up our INLA models, especially because we have the hardware to do so. We have these 56 core Intel Xeon machines with 1TB of memory, and so, my questions 1 through 3 above have been all focused on how I can speed up given my CPU and memory.

However, I happened to get my hands on a local machine with NVIDIA Quadro Pro GPUs. I installed CUDA in it, and have NVBLAS set up, so that I can have it be a drop-in BLAS library when I spin up R with certain flags and configurations. One thing to note is that: NVIDIA does not provide any official LAPACK libraries yet for going through CUDA, and so: at best, I can have an R session with CUDA BLAS and MKL LAPACK.

Here's the question I am really curious on: would anyone here happen to have any experience with beefing up INLA with GPUs, as far as the backend goes?? From reading the Makefile, it looks like INLA relies on LAPACK libraries and so maybe that's why this is not possible yet. But, if there was a way to leverage and link the INLA program with GPUs and make math go fast, then I would be very very happy...

I have been emailing the R HPC mailing list, which is where I learned about the drop-in BLAS solution for CUDA, but no one addressed anything about INLA specifically. If anyone here has happened to do any research on it, then I'd be forever grateful if you could share your knowledge!!!

Thank you so much reading this!

Nafis

> 2) blas.num.threads: Suppose that I built INLA by successfully
> linking against the MKL libraries, and R is also loaded up with the
> proper Intel MKL BLAS/LAPACK (which I can confirm from
> sessionInfo()). Would having the `blas.num.threads` option set to
> something more than 1 get INLA to use MKL threading?

I think so, all this is a little unclear to me. the inla-program turn
off nested parallelism in the openmp, so I'm not sure how openblas/mkl
reacts to that.

>
> 3) On the topic of parallelization: I have seen in simple examples
> that if I set `num.threads` to more than 1, then INLA will use OpenMP
> threading to fit a model, and that can be faster. However, it looks
> like when I have a model with a large spatial region and therefore a
> large number of random effects, INLA will segfault if I set OpenMP to
> more than 1. I have tried this on a machine with 1TB of memory.

that should not happen, if it does, there should be another
explanation. For larger models, there is little potensial
as the default TAUCS library factorise sparse matrices in serial, and
there are few good parallel libraries for sparse-matrices around.

the collaboration with the PARDISO developers, is very promising, see
the output of

inla.pardiso()

which can be used to push the limits. We have ran models with millions
of nodes using pardiso.parallel strategy (see the info in the prev
command).

You'll need an license though. Its free for academic use. Not windows
yet, though. (I havn't got the linking stuff to work yet...)

This is the only option for the moment, and the only option to
do this better for larger models/more cores.

On Linux and Mac, then the pardiso library is loaded if you request it,
otherwise, a fake one is loaded. this happens when then program starts
and is defined in the run-scripts above.

Note that, if you compile yourself, you have to remove the libpardiso.o
file in inlaprog/src when linking the inla program, and load a shared
object library with the same name (either with PARDISO
or without PARDISO). which copies you'll find in the installed R-INLA
files, like

$ ls R/x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu-library/default/INLA/bin/pardiso/
libnopardiso/  libpardiso/

> My assumption here is that: as we set higher number of `num.threads`
> to, let's say, 4, INLA will try to estimate 4 times the number of
> parameters and therefore, there might be some internal limits to the
> number of parameters that is being hit, even though the memory limit
> is not being reached at all. Is that a correct assumption? And if so,
> do you have any other suggestions of speeding up the computation
> beyond just jacking up OpenMP threading?

If you not using PARDISO in pardiso.parallel mode, then it actually cap
the number of threads, like with M hyperparameters, it uses

	MIN(M+1, omp_get_max_threads())

but this various throughout the code, and for the numerical
integration, it can potentially all threads.

>
>
> 4) Finally, GPUs! : Ultimately, the end goal of this research for me
> is to see how much I can speed up our INLA models, especially because we have the hardware to do so. We have these 56 core Intel Xeon machines with 1TB of memory, and so, my questions 1 through 3 above have been all focused on how I can speed up given my CPU and memory.

> does not provide any official LAPACK libraries yet for going through
> CUDA, and so: at best, I can have an R session with CUDA BLAS and MKL
> LAPACK.

I have no experience in that direction. If you have, it would be useful
if you could share them.

> Here's the question I am really curious on: would anyone here happen
> to have any experience with beefing up INLA with GPUs, as far as the
> backend goes??

None that I am aware of.

Hope this helps,

H

You can fix the hyper-parameter, e.g. to prevent overfitting. But shrinkage priors are better. See
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic115.html#52_fix_(theta_1)_and_look_the_result

Hi,

the PARDISO integration is kind of experimental for the moment, and by
default, INLA is set up to compile and link with open-source software
only

to link with the PARDISO library, do

in inlaprog/Makefile, remove in the 'OBJ=' definition, the entry
'src/libpardiso.o'

add linking to either

R/x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu-
library/default/INLA/bin/pardiso/libnopardiso/linux/libpardiso.so

R/x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu-
library/default/INLA/bin/pardiso/libpardiso/linux/libpardiso.so

which you'll find in your own R-INLA installation.

INLA needs a special version of the PARDISO library, and that is only
distributed with the INLA package. downloading from their website will
not work.

the PARDISO library in the INLA pacakge, is compiled with gcc-7.2
compilers (Ubuntu1804) if you want the ones compiled with gcc-4.8
(Ubuntu1604, centOS7), you have to download the linux binary from

http://inla.r-inla-download.org/Linux-builds/

and use the libpardiso.so  in there.

Best
H

--
Håvard Rue

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I have a question about the nested effects. Say I want to get the non-linear effect of covariate x for each season in two different cities, i.e. "x | city / season".

Right now, I create a new index: 1 = season 1 in city 1, 2 = season 2 in city 1, 3 = season 3 in city 1, 4 = season 4 in city 1,  5 = season 1 in city 2, 6 = season 2 in city 2, 7 = season 3 in city 2, 8 = season 4 in city 2.

I write the formula as:
form <- y ~ 0 + f(x, replicate=index, model='rw1')

So I am taking the eight groups (4 seasons * 2 cities) totally separately, but how can I specify that group 1-4 belong to city 1, group 5-8 belong to city 2?

Thank you in advance!

Rujia

On Sunday, March 17, 2019 at 9:19:37 PM UTC-4, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Hi,
>
> it depends on what precisely the "nested" aspect should mean; someone
> with familiarity of lme4 might have a clearer answer to this,
> but my understanding is that "(1 | area / site)" is equivalent to "(1
> | area) + (1 | area:site)". However, the interaction term "area:site"
> seems to me to be equivalent to just "site", since each site can only
> be located within one of your two areas. That would indicate that
> f(area) + f(site) is what you need.
>
> An exception to that would be if the lme4 "(1 | area:site)" implies
> that each area should have its own variance parameter for the
> area:site effect. If that's the case, I believe you would need
> to split the site index vector into site1 and site2; if
>   area = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2)
> and
>  site <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
> let
>  site1 <- site2 <- site
>  site1[area != 1] <- NA # site1: c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, NA, NA)
>  site2[area != 2] <- NA # site1: c(NA, NA, 3, NA, 5, 6, 7)
> and use
>  f(area) + f(site1, n = 7) + f(site2, n = 7)
> in the formula, so that each area gets it's own iid-precision
> parameter for the site effects.
>
> For a smaller computational model the site indices within site1 and
> site2 should be compressed into
>  site1: c(1, 2, NA, 3, NA, NA, NA)
>  site2: c(NA, NA, 1, NA, 2, 3, 4)
> and the "n" parameters to f can be removed.
>
> If there are no repeated measurements, this is easily done:
>  site1 <- site2 <- site
>  site1[area != 1] <- NA
>  site2[area != 2] <- NA
>  site1[area == 1] <- seq_len(sum(area == 1))
>  site2[area == 2] <- seq_len(sum(area == 2))
>
> If there _are_ repeated measurements, more care needs to be taken when
> renumbering the sites, so that all observations for a site is mapped
> to the same new index.
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 18 Mar 2019 at 00:20, <attn...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I have count data from multiple sites (e.g. S1, S2, S3, S4) which are located in two areas ("north", "south"), with a pile of continuous covariates, and multiple years (modelled with "rw2").
> >
> > How would I specify the model to indicate that sites 1 & 2 are always in "north" area and sites 3 & 4 are always in "south" area ?
> >
> > I've tried the following specifications (leaving out model = "iid" from each term for clarity):
> >
> > f1 = count ~ f(area) + f(site) + cov
> > f2 = count ~ f(area, site) + cov
> > f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(area2, site) + cov  # area2 being a duplicate of area
> > f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(site, area2) + cov
> >
> > In lme4 I'd specify: count ~ cov + (1 | area / site)
> >
> > Which, if any, is the correct INLA specification?
> >
> > (Please excuse the basic question--I'm brand new to R-INLA, but enjoying it so far!)
> >

messages.body_plain:
Ok, so the maths doesn't indicate that you want the random effect
variance \sigma^2 to be diffrent for each city, but your text does say
that.
I think Haavard commented on this in another list email recently. The
basic approach would be to have one f() per city, since that would
give you different sigma for each city.
But that can easily be a lot of variance parameters with many cities,
so I woulnd't recommend that unless the number of cities is small (2-4
perhaps, but that's depending on problem size)

Finn

Finn

In addition to what others have said, in the book by Wang et al. (page 120) they describe how to fit near mixed models using the 'lmer' function to define the matrices of fixed and random effects and INLA latent effect 'z'. You may also find this interesting:

https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-multilevel.html

Here, 'model.matrix' is used to define the matrices of random effects, which requires a formula and a data.frame and simplifies the model definition.

Best,

Virgilio

model {

    W[j] ~ dpois(muP[j])
   }
}

messages.subject: Re utilising higher-order adjacency neighbours in BYM model
messages.subject_clean: Re utilising higher-order adjacency neighbours in BYM model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question regarding fitting a BYM model that utilises higher-order adjacency neighbours.

My code attached examines the London suicides data. I use poly2nb() and nblags() (spdep package) to construct 1st-, 2nd-, and 10th-order neighbour adjacency objects, and convert these for use in inla() using nb2INLA(). Each model is fitted using:

formulaX <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adjX)
modX <- inla(formula1,family="poisson",data=data,E=E)

I then extract either the spatial component (zeta) or the fitted values using:

zetaX <- unname(sapply(modX$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas],function(x)inla.emarginal(exp,x)))
fittedX <- unname(sapply(modX$marginals.linear.predictor,function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x)))

My question is: as I increase the contiguity order, I expect a greater degree of smoothing. In particular for the extreme 10th-order model, I expected both the zeta values and fitted values of all polygons to be smoothed to approximately the same value (since there are only 32 polygons in total). However, I observe almost no difference in the zeta & fitted values for a particular polygon as I change the order of the neighbourhood file (both maps attached).

I think I am perhaps not understanding either:

a) a fundamental property of the BYM model, e.g. that higher-order neighbourhood specifications are not allowed (though I understand the opposite from the literature, e.g. see Duncan et al. Int J Health Geogr (2017) 16:47 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12942-017-0120-x), or
b) something under the hood of INLA, e.g. that higher-order graph files should not be created using nblags(), but by some other means..

Can anyone advise?

Thank you,
Matt

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re utilising higher-order adjacency neighbours in BYM model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re utilising higher-order adjacency neighbours in BYM model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think the issue is that to get increased smoothing when you increase
the number of neigh's, you also have to increase the smoothness of the
model. In your case, the smoothness of the model, is kept the same, but
you vary only the number of neighbours.

It's a little like (not the same!), as approximating a derivative f'(x)
with 2 points, 3 points, 5 points, 7 points, .. you still get the same
derivative.

the model='besag' is explained well in the chapter 3 in the GMRF book.
and also how to construct higher order models.

Best
H

On Thu, 2019-03-28 at 21:12 -0700, Matt Tuson wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I have a question regarding fitting a BYM model that utilises higher-
> order adjacency neighbours.
>
> My code attached examines the London suicides data. I use poly2nb()
> and nblags() (spdep package) to construct 1st-, 2nd-, and 10th-order
> neighbour adjacency objects, and convert these for use in inla()
> using nb2INLA(). Each model is fitted using:
>
> formulaX <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adjX)
> modX <- inla(formula1,family="poisson",data=data,E=E)
>
> I then extract either the spatial component (zeta) or the fitted
> values using:
>
> zetaX <-
> unname(sapply(modX$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas],function(x)inla.emar
> ginal(exp,x)))
> fittedX <- unname(sapply(modX$marginals.linear.predictor,function(x)
> inla.emarginal(exp,x)))
>
> My question is: as I increase the contiguity order, I expect a
> greater degree of smoothing. In particular for the extreme 10th-order
> model, I expected both the zeta values and fitted values of all
> polygons to be smoothed to approximately the same value (since there
> are only 32 polygons in total). However, I observe almost no
> difference in the zeta & fitted values for a particular polygon as I
> change the order of the neighbourhood file (both maps attached).
>
> I think I am perhaps not understanding either:
>
> a) a fundamental property of the BYM model, e.g. that higher-order
> neighbourhood specifications are not allowed (though I understand the
> opposite from the literature, e.g. see Duncan et al. Int J Health
> Geogr (2017) 16:47 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12942-017-0120-x), or
> b) something under the hood of INLA, e.g. that higher-order graph
> files should not be created using nblags(), but by some other means..
>
> Can anyone advise?
>
> Thank you,
> Matt
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Haavard,

Thank you for the reference. I think I understand the ideas in chapter 3, in particular that greater smoothing may be achieved by, for example, incorporating distance between nodes (as for Germany in example 3.6).

However it is unclear to me how to bring those ideas to the r-inla framework, and how to combine with higher-order neighbours. Is it that to achieve greater smoothing I should step away from the BYM specification? Or that I may stay with BYM but manipulate the prior specification for the "besag" component appropriately? I have tried a several values for the BYM priors (via hyper=list(prec.unstruct=...,prec.spatial=...)) yet still observe very little difference in the fitted values.

If you can point me towards any r-inla code samples that achieves greater/less smoothing in my context that would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,
Matt

Dear INLA Forum

Whether INLA can be used to solve the multicollinearity and measurement error simultaneously because to solve multicollinearity and measurement error need latent approach (i.e Bayesian ridge regression).  I have climate variables where the variables have high collinearity and there are indications of measurement errors. I read in Wang (2018), we can use Ridge regression approach to overcome the collinearity and model="mec" to solve the classical measurement error. However, those problems need latent approach. Is it possible to overcome those problems simultaneously?

messages.subject: RE: [r-inla] Bayesian ridge regression and measurement error model in X
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Bayesian ridge regression and measurement error model in X
messages.body_plain:
Mindra:

INLA’s default prior on all fixed effects is a diffuse Gaussian prior centered at 0.  So, provided your predictors have been centered at zero, which is a good idea regardless of modeling method, INLA effectively imposes some form of ridge regression on any model, at least in my opinion.

The effectiveness of the ridge prior can depend on the spread component.  The default prior in INLA is on the precision, and is extremely diffuse.  Canonical ridge regression would set the prior on the precision to be 1 (identical to the variance, as its reciprocal).  If your predictors are scaled to the unit interval (0,1), which again is usually a good idea regardless, this is easy to apply across the board by just setting the default INLA prior on the precision of the fixed effects (control.fixed) to 1.  I would try that and see how it works. You can then monitor the marginal likelihoods to see how further adjustments to the spread (raising or lowering it) affects accuracy. There are other ways to more formally replicate ridge regression in INLA, but I’m not sure they are worth the additional hassle. Others may disagree.

To the extent you see the need to perform variable selection (forcing some variables to zero, rather than just minimizing their values), you may want to try running the model in Stan and selecting a regularized horseshoe prior.  Once you have selected only the variables you probably want, you can return to INLA to resume ridge regression optimization.

I will defer to others on the measurement error issue.  Measurement error, though, is just sampling predictors from a secondary distribution of the subject measurement with a typically-Gaussian spread of whatever the measurement error is.  I don’t recall whether that function is built in to INLA (I suspect it may be, or least there may be another function that approximates it), but perhaps you could set up a secondary likelihood within the INLA formula to replicate it if need be.

Best,

Jonathan

Dear INLA Forum

Whether INLA can be used to solve the multicollinearity and measurement error simultaneously because to solve multicollinearity and measurement error need latent approach (i.e Bayesian ridge regression).  I have climate variables where the variables have high collinearity and there are indications of measurement errors. I read in Wang (2018), we can use Ridge regression approach to overcome the collinearity and model="mec" to solve the classical measurement error. However, those problems need latent approach. Is it possible to overcome those problems simultaneously?

Thank you very much.

Best

messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard:

After tinkering around with compilations quite a bit, I have been able to successfully link and make PARDISO work. I ended up using the .so file from the testing version, and upgraded my OS and GLIBC so that there's no weird issues like the ones I faced previously.

The biggest success story I saw here is: in one of my colleague's models where it needs to fit roughly 280,000 total parameters, using the general parallelization strategy with even 2 threads (not mentioning any openmp.strategy, and hence defaulting to Taucs) was segfaulting INLA. We were however able to parallelize smaller models, and so that's when I hypothesized that perhaps parallelization is causing some inner limits to be crossed and therefore INLA segfaults immediately before it starts the iteration.

Now with PARDISO (parallel), we actually have been able to get the model running with parallel threads! Which is amazing.

The last thing that this makes me think is: is there perhaps some limits imposed in Taucs that could be causing the segfault? My thinking behind this is that: the only thing that changed between the 2 INLA calls that caused the segfault to go away is the changing of the parallelization strategy. Thoughts?

Nafis

Hi. This is most likely an issue with lack of memory. TAUCS in serial
and was written in long time ago. There will be a limit how far we can
push serial factorisation of a matrix. There is nothing to do really,
except having more memory.

> Now with PARDISO (parallel), we actually have been able to get the
> model running with parallel threads! Which is amazing.

For such cases, the openmp.stratey = "pardiso.parallel"  is the one,
yes. Which take one matrix at the time an apply parallel factorisation.
There should be an intermediate stage, using nested parallelism, but
its not there yet.

> The last thing that this makes me think is: is there perhaps some
> limits imposed in Taucs that could be causing the segfault?

I would not worry to much, as there is nothing to be done in that
direction. TAUCS is serial and there is no way around. The future is
parallel for larger models, only option.

Happy to hear that its working now!

Just recall to link with the MKL libs

H
